choices.feedback: The findings you already have are enough. Waiting for a number before treating poor perfusion wastes scored time and, in the field, the patient.

choices.text: Begin CPR because the pulse is weak and fast
choices.feedback: He has a pulse and is talking. Compressions on a perfusing patient is a dangerous, unnecessary intervention and is itself a critical failure.

steps.prompt: You are performing the rapid trauma exam. You have completed the head and face. The evaluator is watching your sequence and listening to your narration.

choices.text: Neck for tenderness, distended veins and tracheal position, then apply the correctly sized collar, then chest, abdomen, pelvis, all four extremities with pulse, motor and sensation, then log-roll to inspect the back
choices.feedback: Correct, and in the scored order. Say DCAP-BTLS as you palpate each region and call out what you find and what you do not find.

choices.text: Chest, abdomen, pelvis, extremities, back, then return to the neck and apply the collar
choices.feedback: Wrong order. The neck is assessed and the collar applied before you move down, because that is when you have the information the collar decision depends on.

choices.text: Press the pelvis firmly several times to confirm instability
choices.feedback: Harmful. One gentle assessment only, and stop immediately if it is unstable. Repeated pressure can restart bleeding from a pelvic fracture.

choices.text: Assess only the areas the patient reports hurting to save time
choices.feedback: The rapid trauma exam is a full sweep for a significant mechanism. A distracting injury hides others, which is exactly why the sweep exists.

steps.prompt: The exam is complete and the patient is packaged. You have about two minutes of station time remaining. The evaluator asks what you are doing now.

choices.text: Obtain baseline vitals, take a SAMPLE history, repeat the primary survey, and state that you reassess every 5 minutes on an unstable patient
choices.feedback: Correct. These are scored elements, and stating the reassessment interval out loud is what demonstrates it.

choices.text: Announce that the assessment is finished and wait
choices.feedback: Leaves scored points on the table. Vitals, history and reassessment are components of this station.

choices.text: Begin splinting the extremities you found tender
choices.feedback: Wrong priority for a load-and-go patient. Splinting happens en route, if at all, and never delays transport of an unstable trauma patient.

choices.text: Take vitals only, then hand off
choices.feedback: Partial credit at best. History and a repeated primary survey are both part of the sequence.

scenarios.debrief: The trauma station scores a sequence, not a diagnosis. The shape is fixed: precautions and scene size-up out loud, manual spinal stabilization when the mechanism calls for it, a primary survey that fixes each life threat as it is found, a stated transport decision, a full head-to-toe sweep using DCAP-BTLS with the collar applied at the neck, then baseline vitals, SAMPLE history and reassessment every 5 minutes. Notice where the critical failures sit. Two are in the first 30 seconds and consist entirely of things you say. One sits in the middle, where an airway, breathing or circulation finding goes unmanaged. One more is created by you, when an unnecessary or dangerous intervention gets added. The single habit that protects all of them is narration. If the evaluator cannot hear it, you did not do it.

scenarios.title: Skill station: medical assessment, minute by minute
scenarios.intro: You are at the patient assessment and management medical station. The evaluator reads: you are called for a 64-year-old woman with difficulty breathing. She is sitting on the edge of her bed, awake and speaking in short phrases. You have a partner and a full BLS ambulance. This station is driven by history rather than a head-to-toe sweep, and the evaluator will provide findings only when you ask for them specifically.

choices.text: Verbalize standard precautions, confirm scene safety, note the number of patients and the nature of the illness, and consider additional resources
choices.feedback: Correct. The opening 30 seconds is identical in both assessment stations, and both items are listed critical criteria.

choices.text: Ask the patient to describe her breathing problem
choices.feedback: You skipped the scored opening. Precautions and scene safety come before patient contact in every station.

choices.text: Apply oxygen immediately because she is short of breath
choices.feedback: Premature and out of sequence. You have not assessed adequacy of breathing or her saturation, and you have not stated precautions.

choices.text: Ask the evaluator whether the scene is safe and put on gloves
choices.feedback: Half right. Add eye protection and state the nature of illness, patient count and resource needs to complete the size-up.

steps.prompt: The scene is safe. She is alert and oriented, speaking in three-word phrases, sitting upright and leaning forward.

choices.text: Complete the primary survey: general impression, level of consciousness, airway, breathing with an intervention for the low saturation, and circulation, then state a transport priority
choices.feedback: Correct. The primary survey comes before the history in both stations, and low saturation with increased work of breathing is treated as you find it.

choices.text: Begin OPQRST immediately since this is a medical patient
choices.feedback: History is the core of this station but it does not replace the primary survey. Life threats first, story second.

choices.text: Perform a rapid head-to-toe exam
choices.feedback: That belongs to the trauma station. In a medical patient, the history tells you which system to examine.

choices.text: Assist ventilations with a bag-valve mask
choices.feedback: Too aggressive for these findings. She is alert, speaking and moving air, so oxygen and further assessment come first; she may need CPAP, not a bag.

steps.prompt: Oxygen is applied. The evaluator waits for you to build the story.

choices.text: Take OPQRST on the dyspnea, then a full SAMPLE history including medications and the events leading up to today
choices.feedback: Correct and in the scored order. Ask about onset, what makes it better or worse, what it feels like, whether anything else hurts, severity, and how long, then work SAMPLE.

choices.text: Ask only whether she has a history of asthma
choices.feedback: Far too narrow. A single closed question cannot separate heart failure, COPD, pneumonia and pulmonary embolism, and the station scores the full history.

choices.text: Skip the history and take vitals, since she is short of breath
choices.feedback: Reverses the station. The history drives the focused exam and the field impression, both of which are scored.

choices.text: Ask the family for the history instead of the patient
choices.feedback: Useful supplementation, not a substitute. She is alert and oriented, so she is the primary source.

steps.prompt: She has had worsening breathlessness over three days, cannot lie flat, sleeps on three pillows instead of one, and takes furosemide and lisinopril. Her ankles are swollen.

choices.text: Perform a focused exam of the respiratory and cardiovascular systems: breath sounds in all fields, work of breathing, neck veins, peripheral edema, and pulses
choices.feedback: Correct. The history pointed at the heart and lungs, so that is what you examine, and you say why you are examining it.

choices.text: Perform a complete head-to-toe examination for thoroughness
choices.feedback: Thorough is not the same as scored. A focused exam driven by the history is what this station is testing.

choices.text: Auscultate the anterior chest only and move on
choices.feedback: Incomplete. Crackles begin at the bases, and posterior and lateral fields are where you hear them first.

choices.text: Assist her with a bronchodilator because she is wheezing slightly
choices.feedback: Premature and possibly wrong. Wheezing with orthopnea, edema and diuretic use points at heart failure, and reaching for a drug before the exam is finished skips the reasoning being scored.

steps.prompt: You find crackles to the mid-fields bilaterally, distended neck veins, and pitting edema to both ankles. The evaluator asks for your field impression and plan.

choices.text: State acute decompensated heart failure with pulmonary edema, describe upright positioning, oxygen titrated to target, CPAP if she meets the criteria and protocol allows, blood pressure every 5 minutes, and rapid transport with reassessment
choices.feedback: Correct. A named impression with a plan, including the criteria you checked before choosing CPAP, is exactly what the station wants to hear.

choices.text: State that she is short of breath and needs transport
choices.feedback: Not an impression. The station scores your ability to name what you think is happening and justify the treatment that follows from it.

choices.text: State asthma exacerbation and plan a bronchodilator
choices.feedback: Misreads the story. A first asthma attack at 64 with orthopnea, edema, distended neck veins and diuretics is heart failure until proven otherwise.

choices.text: State possible heart failure and plan oxygen and transport without mentioning positioning or reassessment
choices.feedback: Right impression, incomplete plan. Upright positioning is treatment in pulmonary edema, and reassessment intervals are a scored element.

scenarios.debrief: The two assessment stations share an opening and then diverge. Both begin with precautions, scene safety and a primary survey that treats what it finds. From there the trauma station sweeps the body to find injuries, and the medical station builds a story and then confirms it with a focused exam. Running the wrong shape, a head-to-toe on a dyspneic patient or a single closed question instead of a real history, costs points even when the medicine is right. Three habits carry this station. Ask OPQRST and SAMPLE completely, because the evaluator only gives you findings you ask for specifically. Examine the system the history points at and say why you are examining it. Finish with a named field impression and a plan that includes positioning, the oxygen target, any medication with the contraindications you screened, and how often you will reassess.
